reference.source: Clinical genetics and ophthalmic genetics references
clinicalPearls: The commonest form of Stickler syndrome; autosomal dominant, caused by COL2A1 mutations that usually act through haploinsufficiency of type II collagen.
The membranous congenital vitreous anomaly is characteristic of type 1 and helps distinguish it from the beaded vitreous of type 2.
Myopia is typically high, congenital and largely non-progressive, with a high lifetime risk of giant retinal tears and retinal detachment.
Orofacial features include the Pierre Robin sequence (micrognathia, glossoptosis, cleft palate), midface hypoplasia and a flat facial profile.
Sensorineural hearing loss, often high-frequency, and early-onset osteoarthritis with mild epiphyseal dysplasia are common.
Predominantly ocular COL2A1 variants exist, with the eye affected but few systemic features.
Any symptoms of retinal detachment demand urgent ophthalmology; lifelong retinal surveillance is essential.
It sits within the type II collagenopathy spectrum alongside Kniest dysplasia and spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita.
reference.pathophysiology: Stickler syndrome type 1 is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder caused by mutations in COL2A1, which encodes the alpha-1 chain of type II collagen — the predominant fibrillar collagen of hyaline cartilage, the vitreous humour and the nucleus pulposus. Most disease-causing variants are premature stop or frameshift mutations that trigger nonsense-mediated decay, so only a reduced amount of normal type II collagen is produced (haploinsufficiency); this reduced availability disturbs the delicate collagen scaffold of the vitreous, giving the membranous vitreous anomaly and predisposing to vitreoretinal degeneration and retinal detachment, and it impairs cartilage and craniofacial development, producing epiphyseal dysplasia, early osteoarthritis, midface hypoplasia and the Robin sequence. Because type II collagen contributes less to cochlear structures than type XI collagen, hearing loss is usually milder than in the type XI-related forms. The same gene, through different mutation mechanisms, underlies a spectrum of skeletal dysplasias, so genotype and vitreous phenotype together refine the diagnosis.
additionalDifferentials: Stickler syndrome types 2 and 3 (COL11A1 and COL11A2) and recessive forms (COL9A1/2/3)
Kniest dysplasia and spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita (COL2A1 spectrum)
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundoscopy and slit-lamp examination with vitreous phenotyping (membranous anomaly) and refraction
Skeletal survey for epiphyseal and spondyloepiphyseal changes
Cleft palate and airway assessment in infancy
Craniofacial imaging or cephalometry where indicated
redFlags: Symptoms of retinal detachment — flashes, floaters, a visual field shadow or sudden visual loss
Neonatal airway obstruction or feeding difficulty from the Robin sequence
Rapidly worsening myopia or new vitreous haemorrhage
reference.prognosis: Lifespan is normal; the principal threats are retinal detachment (potentially blinding but often preventable with surveillance and timely intervention), progressive hearing loss and early osteoarthritis, all manageable within a multidisciplinary framework.
pitfalls: Underestimating the retinal detachment risk and omitting structured ophthalmic surveillance
Failing to link an apparently isolated Pierre Robin sequence to underlying Stickler syndrome
Attempting to distinguish subtypes without vitreous phenotyping or genetic testing
references: Stickler syndrome surveillance and management guidance
management: Prophylactic retinopexy and prompt surgical repair of giant retinal tears and detachment, the principal preventable morbidity
Structured lifelong ophthalmic surveillance with correction of congenital high myopia and clear detachment safety-netting
Audiological monitoring and hearing aids for sensorineural, often high-frequency, loss
Analgesia, physiotherapy and joint protection for early-onset osteoarthritis and epiphyseal dysplasia
Cleft palate repair and airway management for Pierre Robin sequence in infancy
Genetic counselling and cascade family screening for the autosomal dominant COL2A1 variant
Multidisciplinary coordination across ophthalmology, audiology, clinical genetics and orthopaedics
